As described in the current application, the anesthetizing monitoring unit 110 includes one or more transceivers 104 and processing circuitry 103 with the processor 102 and the memory 106. The anesthetizing monitoring unit 110 is configured to generate a single stimuli signal (Sstimuni) configured to stimulate a motor nerve of a patient. The anesthetizing monitoring unit 110 is further configured to output the generated single stimuli signal (Sstimuii) to stimulating electrodes 122 on a patient 130 via an output port 112 of the anesthetizing monitoring unit 110 to which the stimulating electrodes 122 are connected. The anesthetizing monitoring unit 110 can then receive a response signal (SResponse) from receiving electrodes 121 on the patient 130 at an input port 111 of the anesthetizing monitoring unit 110.

It is submitted that the amended features of independent claim 1 cannot conceivably be performed in the human mind and are therefore not abstract. For instance, generating a single stimuli signal (Sstmuii) configured to stimulate a motor nerve of a patient cannot be conceivably performed in the human mind, nor is generating the particular stimuli signal data performed by generic computer components because the stimuli signal is a particular signal configured for stimulating a patient. Moreover, outputting the generated single stimuli signal to stimulating electrodes on a patient via an output port cannot be conceivably performed in the human mind. Furthermore, receiving a response signal from receiving electrodes on a patient is not something that can be conceivably performed in the human mind. Accordingly, because the above-highlighted features of amended claim 1 cannot, as a practical matter, be performed entirely in a human's mind (even if aided with pen and paper), the above- highlighted features of claim 1 cannot be fairly characterized as a mental process. Analysis: Claim 1 Rejection
Kurtz does not disclose -as set forth in amended claim 1- "estimating a

periodic noise waveform." Instead, Kurtz "stimulat[es] the patient with multiple stimuli, obtain[s] multiple time-based data series, each data series synchronized to a single instance of the stimulus, and average[es] the multiple synchronized data series." (Kurtz, paragraph [0006].)

That is, instead of quantifying the noise in a signal and using the quantified noise to remove the noise from the signal, Kurtz averages multiple signals (including both and signal) to average out the noise from the signal. For example, the claimed "periodic noise waveform" may be estimated by using temporal segments of a noise signal (SNoise) that are detected during a time interval (TNoise) not overlapping with a stimuli signal interval (Tstimulus) and the duration of the response signal (TResponse). This subject matter has been included in new claim 17.

Accordingly, since Kurtz relies on averaging multiple time-based data series that each correspond to a stimulus of multiple stimuli applied to the patient to compensate for poor SNR, Kurtz does not disclose or suggest the claim feature of "estimating a periodic noise waveform (Speriodic), having the duration (TResponse), by using temporal segments of a noise signal (SNoise)."

Moreover, Kurtz fails to disclose or suggest the claim feature of "generating the improved response signal (EResponse) by subtracting the noise waveform from the response signal (SResponse)." In the Final Office Action, the Examiner asserts that paragraphs [0056] and [0059] of Kurtz disclose such features. However, this assertion is not supported by the disclosure in those paragraphs. Paragraph [0059] of Kurtz recites in its entirety (emphasis added):
It will be understood that the electrodes receive continuous data,
sometimes referred to as "noisy data" or "noisy signal". For each stimulus,
a synchronized evoked response within the subject's brain will be

generated. Typically, this evoked response will also be detected by the electrodes but is generally hidden in the noisy signal. Embodiments of the system, apparatus and method herein are intended to separate
the evoked response, or stimulus-synchronized component,
(sometimes referred to as a "response") from the non-synchronized

components (i.e. noise). For ease of reference, a portion of the noisy
signal that is expected to include a stimulus-synchronized component is
also sometimes referred to as a "response" and is also referred to as a "sweep". In situations with poor signal to noise ratios (SNR), which are
typical in physiological evoked responses, the detection of whether or not
there is a response in the noisy signal generally involves providing a
plurality of essentially identical stimuli and averaging a plurality of
responses (i.e. portions of the noisy signal) corresponding to the stimuli.
The final waveform or averaged response (sometimes called the "final
response"), is the estimate of the synchronized evoked response, with

reduced noise. It will be understood that the type of evoked response will generally be dependent on the stimulus and on the subject. For example, if a subject cannot hear an auditory stimulus, then there would not be an
evoked response to the auditory stimulus

Gathering a plurality of responses that each correspond to a portion of a noisy signal that is expected to include a stimulus-synchronized component and then averaging the responses to try and reduce the amount of the noise in the response is not the same as the claim feature of "generating the improved response signalSVG {EMBED HERE} 0.1530.693 by subtracting the noise waveform from the response signal (SResponse)." Thedisclosed "reduced noise" in Kurtz is the result of averaging multiple responses to try and reduce the amount of noise in the final waveform, whereas the claimed method involves estimating the periodic noise waveform and then subtracting the noise waveform from the response signal to generate the improved response signal.

The present disclosure has the advantage that noise is estimated and subtracted for each received response (SResponse). This reduces the delay in noise reduction compared to the teaching of Kurtz, where all of the multiple time-based data series needs to be obtained before processing by weighted average can be performed. Further, the present disclosure has the advantage of better performance when the assumption of quasi-stationary noise over the period of the weighted averaging is not true. The present disclosure then adapts to the noise at each received response (SResponse).

As mentioned in the previous response, the anesthetizing monitoring unit 110 has the advantage of adapting to time invariant noise, as a noise estimate may be generated for each stimuli/response. This is especially a problem as the response

signal amplitude diminishes with the application of drugs. In one example, the periodic noise can appear as an interfering signal such that the current amplitude of the response signal appears as a current pulse response corrupted by varying or non- constant amplitude.

Also as mentioned in the previous response, The method and device of Kurtz is configured differently. The method of Kurtz involves generating a plurality of stimuli, receiving a noisy signal (SResponse) related to evoked response to each of the plurality of stimuli. A static matrix is then estimated for the plurality (group) of responses (SResponse), shrink the static matrix, calculate weights based on an inverse of the shrunk statistic matrix, and applying the weights to the plurality of responses to construct a final response.

In view of the above, Kurtz does not disclose or suggest the features as recited in amended independent claim 1. Accordingly, independent claim 1 is patentable over Kurtz, and the dependent claims are patentable for at least the same reasons.

In view of the foregoing, Applicant requests issuance of a notice of allowance. Should the Examiner feel that a telephone interview would be helpful to facilitate favorable prosecution of the above-identified application, the undersigned invites the Examiner to contact the undersigned at the telephone number provided below.

The absence in this reply of any comments on any contentions set forth in the Office Action should not be construed to be an acquiescence therein. Rather, no comment is needed since the rejections should be withdrawn for at least the foregoing reasons.
